title.text: AI that understands language: sort, search, translate and summarise

objects.text: What can AI do with our messages, contracts and calls, in English and in our local languages?

Leading with AI  |  Session 4 of the 15 (Sessions 0 to 14)
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. In Session 3 we learned to judge a prediction: false alarms, misses, and the score on cases the system never saw. Today we turn to the largest pile of information most organisations hold, which is text: messages from customers, contracts, reports and recorded calls, in English and in our own languages.

The question is: what can AI do with them?

We start in a Ugandan legal library, build the four language jobs from drawings, tour six industries, and watch a search find the right clause from a plain description. Then you add a pile of your own text to your portfolio.

title.text: What you will leave with today

objects.text: By the end of today you will have

objects.alt: speech

objects.text: Name the four jobs AI does with language, sort, search by meaning, translate and summarise, and say what each is good and bad at

objects.alt: question

objects.alt: folder

slides.notes:
You will leave able to name the four jobs AI does with language, sort, search by meaning, translate and summarise, and say what each is good and bad at. You will hold the questions that show whether a tool will work on your text and in your languages.

And your portfolio will gain one or two piles of your own text, each with the job you would give it.

title.text:
Your two hours: four language jobs, the industries,
a demonstration, then your own portfolio

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: I show recorded searches and one live translation. You add your own text to your portfolio.

slides.notes:
Ten minutes to recall Session 3 and meet today’s question. Forty minutes on the four language jobs, then six industries and three real cases. Fifteen minutes of demonstration: recorded searches, then one translation done live. A five-minute break. Ten minutes on your people and the questions to ask.

Then twenty-five minutes on your own portfolio, five on your decision and ten to close. First, how today fits, and five words.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  In Session 3, what are the two ways a prediction can be wrong?
2.  Why can “95% accurate” be useless?
3.  Which score should you ask a vendor for first?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 3. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. 

Question one. In Session 3, what are the two ways a prediction can be wrong? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A false alarm: it flags a case that was fine. A miss: it lets through a case it should have caught.

Question two. Why can “95% accurate” be useless? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. When the event is rare, a system that always says “no” scores high and catches nothing.

Question three. Which score should you ask a vendor for first? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. The score on cases the system never saw, and what each kind of mistake costs.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet has it.

title.text: What today builds on, and where it leads

objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14; the gold one is today.

Today uses sorting is prediction from Session 2 and judging accuracy from Session 3.

It adds sort, search by meaning, translate, summarise.

Session 5: from understanding text to writing it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Word
What it means
Classification
Sorting each message into one of a few labels, such as order, payment or complaint.
Semantic search
Search by meaning: finding the passage that means the same thing, even in different words.
Embedding
A text’s position on a map of meaning, worked out by a model. Close positions mean close meanings.
Machine translation
AI that turns text in one language into text in another.
Low-resource language
A language with little written text online for AI to learn from, as with most Ugandan languages.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. We use every one of them before the end of the session.

title.text:
A customer message is a record too, and it
is sorted and judged as in Sessions 2 and 3

objects.alt: A customer message is a record too, and it is sorted and judged as in Sessions 2 and 3

objects.text: A complaint filed as an order is a miss, as in Session 3.

runs.text: The label is now order, payment or complaint.

slides.notes:
Those five words rest on what you already know. On the left are records from Sessions 2 and 3: a client, a claim, each with a label, a score, and the two ways of being wrong. On the right are three messages from shops to Nile Valley Foods, our fictional distributor.

Each can carry a label too: an order, a complaint, a payment. Sorting messages is the same learning from labelled examples, only the record is now text. And everything Session 3 taught still applies: a complaint filed as an order is a miss. A pile of text becomes a leadership problem when nobody has time to read it, as a Ugandan library shows.

title.text:
ULII in Kampala added AI summaries in 2026 to a
library of 41,000 court decisions few have time to read

objects.alt: ULII in Kampala added AI summaries in 2026 to a library of 41,000 court decisions few have time to read

objects.text: Judges of the Commercial Division were trained to use the summaries.

runs.text: Our question today: what can AI do with our messages, contracts and calls?

slides.notes:
The Uganda Legal Information Institute, ULII, is a free online library of our laws and judgments. It holds more than 41,000 decisions and serves about 350,000 users a month in 45 countries, and some judgments run past fifty pages. By early 2026 it had added AI summaries of long judgments, links to the laws and cases each one cites, and alerts on new decisions, and judges of the Commercial Division were trained to use them.

No accuracy figures have been published yet. Every organisation here has its own version of this pile: messages, contracts, reports and calls. What can AI do with ours?

title.text:
AI does four jobs with language: sort,
search by meaning, translate and summarise

objects.alt: AI does four jobs with language: sort, search by meaning, translate and summarise

objects.text: Calls count as text once speech-to-text from Session 1 has written them out.

runs.text: We take the jobs one at a time, starting with sorting.

slides.notes:
On the left is your text: customer messages, contracts, reports, and calls turned into text, as we saw in Session 1. AI does four jobs with it. It sorts, putting a label on each message, such as order, payment, complaint or urgent. It searches by meaning, so you can describe what you want in ordinary words and find the right clause.

It translates, from English to Luganda or Swahili and back. And it summarises, turning fifty pages into one for a busy reader. We take them one at a time, starting with sorting, because you already know how it works.

title.text:
Sorting puts a label and a score on each
message, and sends the urgent ones to a person

objects.alt: Sorting puts a label and a score on each message, and sends the urgent ones to a person

objects.text: A model learns from past messages that people already sorted.

runs.text: The industry calls this classification.
Judge it on messages it never saw.

slides.notes:
Sorting works as prediction did in Session 2. People sort a few thousand past messages by hand: this one is an order, this a payment, this a complaint. A model learns from them, and then puts a label and a score on every new message as it arrives.

The industry calls this classification. Urgent messages, in the red tray, go straight to a person. And the Session 3 questions all apply. A complaint filed as an order is a miss, and an order flagged urgent is a false alarm. Sorting looks at the words in a message, and words alone can mislead.

title.text:
A flood question and the force majeure clause that
answers it share no word, so word search misses it

objects.alt: A flood question and the force majeure clause that answers it share no word, so word search misses it

objects.text: People link rain, flood and road at once. A word counter does not.

runs.text: Even floods and flood count as different words.
Recorded on ten invented contract clauses.

slides.notes:
A manager asks: what happens if heavy rain floods the road and the delivery cannot get through?

The clause that answers it is force majeure: no party is liable for delay caused by events beyond its control, including flood. You see the link at once. A search that matches words finds nothing, because the question and the clause share no word at all. Even floods and flood count as different words.

That is a recorded run on ten invented contract clauses. For a machine to see that two texts mean the same thing, it needs a different idea of closeness.

title.text:
A model places every text on a map of meaning,
and texts that mean the same sit close together

objects.alt: A model places every text on a map of meaning, and texts that mean the same sit close together

objects.text: A text’s position on the map is called an embedding.

runs.text: A real map has hundreds of directions; this one has two.
Only one question matters: which texts sit closest.

slides.notes:
Picture a map of meaning. A model, trained on a great deal of text, gives every sentence a position on it. Texts about delays and weather land in one corner, payments in another, staff leave in a third. Your flood question lands next to the force majeure clause, even though they share no word, and far from the sick leave policy.

The industry calls a text’s position on this map an embedding. The slide is an illustration with two directions; a real map has hundreds, and nobody reads the positions. We ask one thing of them: which texts sit closest. That gives us a new kind of search.

title.text:
Search by meaning returns the closest passages
first, and a person chooses among them

objects.alt: Search by meaning returns the closest passages first, and a person chooses among them

objects.text: Ask in your own words, as you would ask a colleague.

runs.text: The industry calls it semantic search.
Session 8 builds an assistant on it.

slides.notes:
Search by meaning follows from the map. You ask in your own words. The question is placed on the map, and the passages closest to it come back, nearest first. Then a person reads the top few and chooses. In our recorded run, the flood question brought back force majeure first, then limitation of liability, then indemnity.

The industry calls this semantic search. It lets staff ask a policy manual, a contract library or a knowledge base a question the way they would ask a colleague, and Session 8 builds an assistant on it. Translation, our third job, draws on the same kind of learning.

title.text:
Translation is as good as the text a language has:
English has a library, most of our languages a shelf

objects.alt: Translation is as good as the text a language has: English has a library, most of our languages a shelf

objects.text: These are called low-resource languages.

runs.text: Quality varies by language and topic.
Test with native speakers before anyone relies on it.

slides.notes:
Translation, which the industry calls machine translation, comes from a model that learned from huge amounts of text, including text written in two languages side by side. That is the problem for us. English has a vast library to learn from. Luganda, Acholi, Lugbara and most of our languages have a small shelf by comparison.

The industry calls them low-resource languages. So translation and understanding in them are weaker and vary by language and topic. A tool that reads English contracts well may stumble on a Lusoga voice note. Test in your own languages, with native speakers, before anyone relies on it. Africans are building the shelf.

title.text:
Sunbird, Masakhane, Lelapa and Orange
are building AI for African languages

objects.alt: Sunbird, Masakhane, Lelapa and Orange are building AI for African languages

objects.text: Four efforts to fill the shelf, from Kampala to Dakar.

runs.text: Orange’s Wolof and Pulaar work is a plan, announced in 2024.

slides.notes:
Four efforts are worth knowing. Sunbird AI, here in Uganda, built models for Ugandan languages and launched them with the Ministry of ICT in October 2025; we open its story shortly. Masakhane is a volunteer community: more than 400 people in at least 20 countries built 46 open translation test sets for their own languages, so the speakers of a language help build its AI.

Lelapa AI in South Africa made a deliberately small, cheap open model, open meaning anyone may download and run it, as Session 6 explains, for five African languages, and sells a language service to businesses. And Orange announced in 2024 that it is adapting OpenAI and Meta models to Wolof and Pulaar for customer service; those are plans.

title.text:
Summarising saves reading time, and
can drop the one sentence that matters

objects.alt: Summarising saves reading time, and can drop the one sentence that matters

objects.text: A summary is a draft. Read the original for anything you act on.

runs.text: It keeps what looks typical, and can lose the exception, the number or the deadline.

slides.notes:
The fourth job is summarising, and leaders feel it first. A twelve-page supply contract becomes three lines in seconds: delivery within five days, price fixed for twelve months, either side may end it with notice. That saves real time. Now the red words on the left. Halfway down, the contract says, except deliveries to Gulu.

The summary has dropped it. The slide is an illustration, and the risk is real: a summary keeps what looks typical and can lose the exception, the number or the deadline. Treat a summary as a draft, and read the original for anything you act on.

title.text:
Language AI is good at volume and finding by
meaning, and weak on rare cases and our languages

objects.alt: Language AI is good at volume and finding by meaning, and weak on rare cases and our languages

objects.text: Use it for volume and first drafts. Keep people on the rare and the risky.

runs.text: A message mixing English and Luganda in one line is hard for it.

slides.notes:
Taken together, the four jobs show where language AI earns its place. It is good at volume: it reads every message the same way, sorts thousands a day, finds a passage from a description in ordinary words, and gives you a first translation or summary in seconds. It is weak where its library is thin: languages with little text online, sarcasm, slang and messages that mix English and Luganda in one line, the rare kind of message it never saw, and the single exception buried in page nine.

Use it for volume and first drafts, and keep people on the rare and the risky.

title.text:
A South African bank, an Australian telco and a
Kenyan health charity already put language AI to work

objects.alt: A South African bank, an Australian telco and a Kenyan health charity already put language AI to work

objects.text: FMCG is the gap: sorting shops’ WhatsApp orders is common, but no case is published.

slides.notes:
All four jobs appear across the six main industries. In banking, Standard Bank’s staff ask a bot their IT questions in their own words. In telecom, Telstra’s agents search company knowledge by asking, and see a customer’s history in one sentence. In agriculture, Uganda plans to send farmers advice in their own languages through Sunbird’s models.

In FMCG we have no published case yet; the typical use is sorting the orders and complaints shops send by WhatsApp, which is our fictional Nile Valley Foods example later today. In health, Jacaranda Health, which you met in Session 2, sorts mothers’ text messages in English and Swahili by danger signs.

And in the public sector, the UK government reads consultation replies with AI.

title.text:
The UK government’s Consult tool agreed with its experts
more often than the experts agreed with each other

objects.alt: The UK government’s Consult tool agreed with its experts more often than the experts agreed with each other

objects.text: Compare a machine with people, never with perfection.

slides.notes:
The first story is sorting and summarising at scale. A public consultation brings in tens of thousands of written replies, and civil servants must read and group every one. The UK government’s tool, called Consult, reads each reply, sorts it into themes and counts them; staff then check and correct the themes.

For a review of the water industry, it sorted more than 50,000 replies in about two hours, and experts spent 22 hours checking. It agreed with one or both of two expert groups almost 83 per cent of the time. The two expert groups agreed with each other only 55 per cent of the time, which is Session 3 again: compare a machine with people, never with perfection.

title.text:
More than 8,000 Telstra staff now ask the company’s
knowledge in their own words, and calls got shorter

objects.alt: More than 8,000 Telstra staff now ask the company’s knowledge in their own words, and calls got shorter

objects.text: Search by meaning and summary, inside a contact centre.

slides.notes:
The second story is search by meaning inside a contact centre. Telstra’s frontline staff had to find answers across many internal knowledge bases while the customer waited, and read long customer histories. Now they type a question in their own words, and Ask Telstra searches the company’s own knowledge and writes an answer.

A second tool sums up a customer’s recent history in one sentence. By April 2026 more than 8,000 frontline staff used it, and Telstra says average call time fell by over a minute; in the 2023 trial, follow-up contacts fell by 20 per cent. These are company figures, with no independent audit, and the pilot measures were staff surveys.

title.text:
Sunbird AI in Kampala reports the best results in 24
of 31 languages, in tests nobody else has repeated

objects.alt: Sunbird AI in Kampala reports the best results in 24 of 31 languages, in tests nobody else has repeated

objects.text: Building the shelf for our own languages.

slides.notes:
The third story is ours. Global chatbots handle Luganda, Acholi or Lugbara poorly, because so little of their text is online. Sunbird AI in Kampala took an open model from the Chinese company Alibaba and trained it further on Ugandan books, dictionaries and proverbs, and on more than 500 hours of radio talk shows written out as text.

In Sunbird’s own tests the paper claims the best results in 24 of 31 languages, and in translation into English and into local languages it scored above two leading global models. The builder ran the tests, nobody has repeated them, and no user figures exist yet. Test it in your own languages before you rely on it.

title.text:
In recorded runs, a manager describes a passage in
ordinary words and search by meaning tries to find it

objects.text: I will show

objects.alt: In recorded runs, a manager describes a passage in ordinary words and search by meaning tries to find it

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Does the right passage come first, or in the top three?
What word search finds for the same question
Where it slips, and who chooses

slides.notes:
Now search by meaning at work, in recorded runs. I wrote thirty short invented passages for Nile Valley Foods: ten contract clauses, ten finance terms and ten paragraphs of an HR policy. Then I wrote twelve questions the way a manager or an employee would ask them, and noted the right passage for each before running anything.

A free model, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, did the search by meaning, and a word search ran alongside for comparison. These were recorded on 6 November 2026. Watch whether the right passage comes first or in the top three, what word search finds, and where it slips.

title.text:
Search by meaning puts force majeure first for
the flood question; word search finds nothing

objects.alt: Search by meaning puts force majeure first for the flood question; word search finds nothing

objects.text: All four contract questions found the right clause first. Policies and finance terms were harder.

slides.notes:
The flood question from earlier, run for real. Search by meaning puts force majeure first, then limitation of liability, then indemnity. The bars show how close each clause sat to the question, and force majeure is clearly ahead. On the right, word search finds nothing at all, because no clause shares a word with the question.

A manager who has never heard the words force majeure can still find the clause by describing the problem. Contracts were the easy case, though: all four contract questions found the right clause first. Policies and finance terms were harder.

title.text:
Malaria finds sick leave and theft finds
whistleblowing, but the bank question comes second

objects.alt: Malaria finds sick leave and theft finds whistleblowing, but the bank question comes second

objects.text: Show the top three, and let a person choose.

slides.notes:
Three more questions. An employee writes: I have malaria and cannot come to work tomorrow. Search by meaning finds the sick leave paragraph first, while word search offers the grievance procedure. Another writes: I saw a colleague stealing stock and I am afraid to say so. Meaning finds whistleblowing; word search finds nothing in common.

Then the slip, in red. A finance officer asks: make sure our books match what the bank says. Meaning put bad debt write-off first and the right answer, bank reconciliation, second. A person who sees the top three picks it at once.

title.text:
Across 12 questions the right passage came first 7
times and in the top three 11 times; word search, 4

objects.alt: Across 12 questions the right passage came first 7 times and in the top three 11 times; word search, 4

objects.text: Good enough to shortlist. A person still decides.

runs.text: Twelve questions on thirty passages is a demonstration, too small to be a benchmark.

slides.notes:
Across all twelve, one square per question: search by meaning put the right passage first in 7 and in the top three in 11. Only one, a question about a shop returning damaged bags, missed the top three. Word search put the right passage first in 4. The lesson for a leader is about design: show staff the top three with their sources, and let a person choose.

And treat these twelve questions on thirty short passages as a demonstration only; it is too small to be a benchmark. Your own documents, in your own languages, need their own test. Translation is the job we cannot record in advance.

title.text:
Live, with a fallback, one customer
message goes into Luganda and back

objects.text: I will show

objects.alt: Live, with a fallback, one customer message goes into Luganda and back

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Is the meaning kept?
Do names, amounts and dates survive?
What a Luganda speaker in the room says
If it fails: speakers translate by hand

slides.notes:
This one is live, so neither of us knows the result. I take a short message from a shop, such as: the maize flour was late and the invoice is wrong. I ask a translation tool to put it into Luganda, and I ask a Luganda speaker in the room to read it aloud and tell us whether it sounds right.

Then I translate it back into English and we compare. Watch whether the meaning survives, and whether names, amounts and dates come through intact. If the connection fails, we use Sunbird’s published test results instead, and our Luganda speakers translate by hand. Whatever happens, it is one message, too few to judge a tool.

title.text:
Agents, records staff and legal officers
read less, and judge and correct more

objects.alt: Agents, records staff and legal officers read less, and judge and correct more

objects.text: Jacaranda’s help desk answers the urgent messages first; Telstra’s agents ask instead of hunting.

slides.notes:
Language AI changes your people’s day before it changes your results. A contact-centre agent stops reading and routing every message and spends the time on the urgent, the angry and the unusual. The skill to grow is checking the label and correcting the machine. A records clerk stops hunting through files and becomes the keeper of clean, current documents, because search is only as good as what it searches.

A legal officer stops first-reading every contract and judges the clauses that matter, reading summaries against the original. The fears are real: replaced, sidelined, a dropped clause. What do your agents or clerks fear today?

title.text:
Always leave a customer a door to a person; a Kenyan
petition says Safaricom’s chatbot trapped them

objects.alt: Always leave a customer a door to a person; a Kenyan petition says Safaricom’s chatbot trapped them

objects.text: Sort and answer the routine. Route the rest to a person, fast.

runs.text: A named manager owns the routing rules.

slides.notes:
Whatever your people fear, your customers fear one thing: being stuck with a machine. Design for it. AI sorts each message and answers the routine. The urgent and the unhappy go straight to a person. And any customer can ask for a person at any time, by a route they can see.

In Kenya in April 2026, a petition in the High Court claimed that Safaricom customers are trapped in loops with its Zuri chatbot with no easy way to reach a human. These are claims, with no ruling yet. Whatever the court decides, a named manager should own the routing rules and check every month who waited and why.

title.text:
Six questions that show whether a language tool
will work on your text and in your languages

rows.text: Ask
Why it matters
Which languages does it handle, and was it tested on ours?
Quality falls where a language has little text
How often is it right on our own messages, ones it never saw?
The vendor’s demo text is cleaner than yours
Does it show the top few results and the source passage?
A person can then choose and check
How does it handle slang, spelling slips and mixed languages?
Customers write the way they speak
Where do our messages and documents go, and who can read them?
Contracts and complaints hold personal data
How does a customer reach a person, and how fast?
Loops with no exit lose customers

slides.notes:
Everything so far comes down to six questions, for your own team and for a vendor. Ask which languages the tool handles, and whether it was tested on ours, because quality falls where a language has little text. Ask how often it is right on your own messages, ones it never saw, as in Session 3, since the vendor’s demonstration text is always cleaner than yours.

Ask whether it shows the top few results and the source, so a person can choose. Ask how it handles slang, spelling slips and English and Luganda in one sentence. Ask where your messages and documents go; Session 6 returns to that. And ask how a customer reaches a person.

title.text:
Add one or two piles of your own
text to your AI Opportunity Portfolio

objects.text: 25 minutes
Hands-on: your portfolio
Find a pile of text your organisation struggles to read, and give it a job.

runs.text: Name the pile: messages, contracts, reports or calls.
Fill the five columns, as in the example.
Add today’s column: the job, and the languages.
Write how a person checks the output.

objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: One or two portfolio entries, each with its job, its languages and its check.

slides.notes:
For twenty-five minutes you work on your own organisation, and I walk round. Choose a pile of text your organisation struggles to read: customer messages, contracts, complaints, reports, minutes, recorded calls. Open the AI Opportunity Portfolio in your workbook and fill the five columns: the use, what goes in, what comes out, who uses it, and how you would know it works.

Then today’s column: which of the four jobs, sort, search, translate or summarise, and in which languages. The example on the right is for Nile Valley Foods, our fictional distributor. Finish by writing how a person would check the output each month.

title.text:
Which language job would pay
off first in your organisation?

objects.text: Of the piles of text you just wrote down, which job would you start with, and why?

objects.alt: grid

objects.text: Sort the inbox
Messages and complaints labelled and routed, urgent ones first

objects.alt: magnifier

objects.text: Search our documents
Staff find the policy or clause by asking in their own words

objects.alt: speech

objects.text: Translate or summarise
Reach customers in their language; read long reports faster

objects.alt: clock

objects.text: Not yet
Our documents are scattered, out of date or on paper
Write your decision and the reason in your workbook.

slides.notes:
With your entries written, one decision. Sort the inbox, if messages and complaints pile up and the urgent ones wait too long. Search our documents, if staff waste time hunting for the right policy, product sheet or clause. Translate or summarise, if you need to reach customers in their own language or your managers drown in long reports.

Or not yet, if your documents are scattered, out of date or still on paper. That is a useful answer too, because your first project is then putting the documents in order, which Session 14 covers. Write your choice and the pile it works on, and I will hear a few before we close.

title.text:
Language AI gives you a shortlist,
and a person makes the choice

objects.alt: Language AI gives you a shortlist, and a person makes the choice

objects.text: By meaning, the right passage came first for 7 of 12 questions and in the top three for 11.

runs.text: Sort, search, translate, summarise.
Test in our languages with native speakers.
Always leave customers a door to a person.

slides.notes:
Carry this tally out of the room. Search by meaning found the right passage first for 7 of our 12 questions and in the top three for 11, against 4 for word search, so the design that works is a shortlist with sources and a person who chooses.

Around it sit the rest of today. AI does four jobs with language: it sorts, searches by meaning, translates and summarises, and it sees meaning as closeness on a map. Our languages have less text behind them, so test them with native speakers. And always leave customers a door to a person.

title.text:
Keep the sheet, and the pile of
text you added to your portfolio

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: A one-page sheet: the four language jobs, the map of meaning, today’s recorded search results, the questions to ask, and your new portfolio entries.

objects.text: Our question today
What can AI do with our messages, contracts and calls, in English and in our local languages?
Next session
Session 5: Generative AI: how chatbots write, and why they sometimes invent.

objects.alt: What you keep from today

slides.notes:
